Roof Flashing Repair: Where Flashing Goes and Why It Fails

Most roof leaks start at a joint, not in the middle of the shingles. Call one free number at any hour and you are put through to an independent, locally owned roofing company that repairs flashing across greater Houston.

Call (832) 662-4107 Flashing locations table
  1. Home
  2. Services
  3. Flashing Repair

Flashing is the metal that seals the joints

Ask where flashing goes on a roof and the short answer is: everywhere the roof stops being a plain sheet of shingles. Walls, chimneys, valleys, edges, pipes and skylights all break the surface, and at each one a piece of shaped metal (or a rubber boot) steers water back onto the shingles and down to the gutter.

Because these joints are where two different materials meet, and because they move as the house heats and cools, they are where most roof leaks begin. The shingles around a failed piece of flashing can be in perfect shape. This page shows each place flashing belongs, how a roofer tells it has failed, and what a proper flashing repair involves.

Houston Expert Roofers does not repair flashing. Dial its free number at any hour and an automated assistant connects the call with an independent, locally owned roofing company, which inspects the roof, quotes the repair and does the work.

Every place flashing goes on a roof

A typical Houston house with a two-story wall, a fireplace chimney and a few plumbing vents has most of these. Use the table to match a leak's location to the flashing above it.

FlashingWhere it goesHow it worksCommon failure
Step flashingAlong a sidewall or the sides of a chimney, where the roof slope runs alongside a vertical surfaceAn L-shaped piece is woven in with each shingle course, so every piece laps over the one belowOne long piece face-nailed or caulked instead of individual steps; pieces left out when a roof was redone
CounterflashingOver the top of step or base flashing on chimneys and masonry wallsSet into a cut mortar joint and folded down over the step flashing so water on the brick cannot get behind itPulled out of the joint, or replaced by metal caulked to the brick face
Apron (headwall) flashingWhere the top of a roof slope butts into a wall, or the front of a chimneyA continuous piece laps over the top course of shingles and up the wallSeal at the wall fails; siding or stucco installed without covering the upturned leg
Chimney cricket (saddle)On the uphill side of a chimneyA small peaked ridge that splits water around the chimney so it does not pond behind itMissing on wide chimneys, or its own flashing joints fail
Valley flashingWhere two roof slopes meet in a channelA metal liner (open valley) or woven or cut shingles over a membrane carry water from both slopesDebris dams the valley; worn metal; nails driven too close to the center
Drip edgeAlong the eaves (the bottom edges) and rakes (the sloped side edges)An angled metal edge kicks water away from the fascia and keeps it from wicking back under the shinglesMissing on older roofs, or pieces not lapped, so the fascia and deck edge rot
Kickout (diverter) flashingAt the bottom of a roof-to-wall joint, where the eave meets a sidewallTurns water coming down the wall flashing out into the gutterMissing, so water runs behind siding or brick and rots the wall below
Pipe boots and vent flashingAround plumbing vents, exhaust vents and other pipes through the roofA metal flange under the upper shingles with a rubber or lead collar that grips the pipeRubber collar cracks in sun and heat; flange lifted by a nail pop
Skylight flashingAll four sides of a skylightStep flashing on the sides, a head piece at the top and an apron at the bottom, usually as a kitLeaks at the uphill head where water and debris collect

What the building code says about flashing

The City of Houston adopted the 2021 International Residential Code, with local amendments, for work from January 2024, and many surrounding cities use the same model code. The code sets the minimum, and the shingle maker's installation instructions add their own requirements. A few flashing rules that come up often:

Drip edge on shingle roofs

The residential code requires drip edge at the eaves and rake edges of asphalt shingle roofs (section R905.2.8.5), with adjoining pieces lapped at least two inches, the metal extending at least a quarter inch below the deck edge, and fasteners no more than 12 inches apart. Underlayment laps over the drip edge at the eaves and runs under it at the rakes.

Diverter flashing at roof-to-wall joints

Section R903.2.1 calls for flashing where a roof meets a wall and for a diverter that sends water away where the eave of a sloped roof meets a vertical sidewall. The code does not use the word "kickout", which may be one reason this piece is so often missing.

Sidewall base flashing

Base flashing against a sidewall must be continuous or step flashing at least 4 inches high and 4 inches wide (section R905.2.8.3), directing water onto the roof or into the gutter. Where there is siding, the upturned leg runs up behind it.

Crickets behind wide chimneys

A cricket or saddle is required on the ridge side of any chimney or penetration more than 30 inches wide measured across the slope (section R903.2.2), covered in sheet metal or the same material as the roof.

Code language changes between editions, and cities amend it, so treat this as background. The roofer and your city's permit office decide what applies to a specific job.

Why caulk is not flashing

Flashing keeps water out by overlapping. Each piece sits under the material uphill of it and over the material downhill of it, the way shingles do, so water always runs out across a surface instead of into a seam. That works even when every seal in the joint has failed.

Caulk and roofing cement work the opposite way: they only keep water out while they stay stuck to both surfaces. Houston sun, heat and the daily movement of metal against brick or wood pull them loose over time. That is why a thick bead of sealant at a wall or chimney is usually a sign of an earlier patch over a flashing problem, not a repair.

Sealant still has a place. It is used at exposed fastener heads and in the reglet where counterflashing meets brick, and a roofer may smear it on as a temporary measure after a storm. If an estimate says "seal" or "caulk" at a leaking joint, ask whether that is the whole repair or a stopgap until the flashing can be replaced.

Signs a flashing joint has failed

  • A ceiling or wall stain near an outside wall, a chimney or a skylight, keeping in mind water can run several feet before it drips.
  • Leaks that appear in wind-driven rain but not in a steady, straight-down rain.
  • Rust streaks on the shingles below a chimney, vent or wall joint.
  • Thick caulk or black tar visible at a joint from the ground, meaning someone has already patched it.
  • Stained, swollen or soft siding or trim below the bottom of a roof-to-wall joint, which points to a missing kickout.
  • Damp or stained drywall around a fireplace, often blamed on the chimney itself.

Look from the ground or through a window only. Binoculars help. Do not climb onto the roof or lean a ladder against a gutter to look, and leave the close inspection to the roofer.

Stay off the roof. Wet, storm-damaged roofs are slick and the decking may be weak, so leave the ladder in the garage. Keep well away from downed power lines and report them to CenterPoint Energy or 911. Indoors, move belongings away from the leak, put a bucket or towels under the drip and keep people out of any room where the ceiling sags. Photograph the damage from the ground and inside the house, then call your insurer and a roofer.

How a careful roofer repairs flashing

  1. Confirm the source. The roofer checks the attic or the inside of the wall and the joint itself to make sure the water starts at the flashing, not at a nearby boot or valley.
  2. Lift the shingles around the joint. Step flashing is woven into the shingle courses, so the shingles next to the wall or chimney have to come up, carefully, to reach it.
  3. Check the wood underneath. Long-running flashing leaks often rot the deck edge or the wall sheathing. Soft wood should be replaced before new metal goes in.
  4. Install new metal the right way. Individual step pieces with each course, counterflashing cut into the mortar on masonry, a kickout at the bottom of wall joints, and new boots on vents.
  5. Relay and match the shingles. The roofer should say beforehand whether it can reuse or match your shingles, and should photograph the work before the shingles cover it.

On a roof with years of life left, replacing flashing alone is usually the right call. If the roof is close to replacement anyway, ask whether it makes more sense to fold the flashing into a new roof, since a full replacement should include new flashing. The roof leak repair page covers leaks from other sources.

What drives the cost of a flashing repair

The line does not quote prices, and a figure without seeing the roof would not be honest. These are the things a roofer weighs when it prices the job, so you can understand why two flashing repairs on the same street can cost very different amounts.

Location and access

A pipe boot on a low, walkable slope is quicker than a chimney on a steep second-story roof, which may need extra safety gear and time.

How much roofing comes up

Step flashing along a long wall means lifting and relaying many courses of shingles, and brittle older shingles may need replacing rather than relaying.

Masonry and siding

Counterflashing on brick means cutting and sealing mortar joints. On walls, siding or trim may have to come off to fit the flashing behind it.

Hidden rot

Rotten decking or wall sheathing found under the old flashing adds to the job. Ask for a unit price for any wood replaced.

Materials

Galvanized steel, aluminum, copper and lead behave and cost differently, and matching existing metal on an older home can matter.

Matching shingles

If your shingle is discontinued, the roofer may need to discuss alternatives before it starts lifting courses.

Texas has no state roofing license. No state agency licenses roofing contractors in Texas, and a 2025 bill to create one (HB 3344) did not reach a vote of the full House before the session ended. So check what you can: a certificate of liability insurance sent to you, a written contract with the full scope, a permit where your city requires one, local addresses you can drive past, and the shingle maker's warranty registration. Questions Houston homeowners ask

Where does flashing go on a roof?

Flashing goes wherever the roof is interrupted or meets something else: along walls (step flashing, with counterflashing or siding over it), where a roof meets a wall at its top edge (apron or headwall flashing), around chimneys (step flashing, counterflashing and a cricket on the uphill side of wider chimneys), in valleys, at eaves and rakes (drip edge), at the bottom of a roof-to-wall joint (kickout flashing), and around pipes, vents and skylights. The table on this page lists each one.

How much is flashing for a roof?

The line does not quote prices, and there is no fair single figure. What drives the cost is where the flashing is (a pipe boot on a low slope is simpler than a chimney on a steep one), how many shingles must be lifted and relaid around it, the metal used, whether bricks need new mortar joints for counterflashing, and whether rotten decking turns up underneath. Ask the roofer for a written estimate that names each flashing part it will replace.

Can caulk or roofing cement replace flashing?

No. Sealant can buy time in an emergency, but it is not flashing. Flashing works by lapping metal under and over the roofing so water is shed downhill even if a seal fails. Caulk only works while it stays stuck, and Houston sun and heat break it down. If you see a thick bead of caulk or tar at a wall or chimney, that is usually a sign someone patched a flashing problem instead of fixing it.

Should flashing be replaced when I get a new roof?

Ask the roofer to quote new flashing and pipe boots with any replacement, or to explain in writing why it plans to reuse a piece. Counterflashing set into a chimney's mortar is sometimes left in place if it is sound. Reusing old, rusted or bent step flashing under brand new shingles is a common cause of the first leak on a new roof. The roof replacement page lists what a full quote should include.

What is kickout flashing and do I need it?

A kickout (also called a diverter) is a bent piece of metal at the bottom of the joint where a roof edge runs into a wall. It turns the water flowing down the wall flashing out into the gutter instead of letting it run behind the siding or brick. The International Residential Code calls for this kind of diverter flashing where a roof eave meets a sidewall. Missing kickouts often show up as stained or rotten siding below the joint.
